papers.title: TAC2: Timestamped Audio Captioning as composable functions
papers.abstract: Real-world audio applications require precise, queryable representations grounded in physical time. Yet modern Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) increasingly favor conversational generation, producing free-form descriptions that conflate acoustic perception with higher-level reasoning and lack precise temporal grounding. We introduce TAC2, a foundation model that casts timestamped audio captioning as composable functions to construct granular, speaker-attributed acoustic timelines directly from in-the-wild audio. To avoid prohibitively expensive manual annotation, we programmatically fuse complementary predictions from specialized weak teachers through time-registered IoU matching. We model the resulting multi-granularity schema of timestamped events, speaker turns, and fine-grained speech attributes using an Instruction-Input-Output (IIO) completion format, in which each task is a function of the audio, an instruction, and an optional input. A single call decodes the full description autonomously, while composing calls lets earlier outputs or external priors, such as a reference transcript, condition later ones. We further extend TAC2 with expressive speech attributes to obtain TAC2-S, using parameter-efficient specialists to elicit latent paralinguistic capabilities from the pre-trained backbone and distill them into a unified model. We validate the resulting representation in two complementary settings. Paired with frozen text-only LLMs, it yields strong spoken audio understanding across diverse reasoning backends, demonstrating the utility of decoupling fine-grained acoustic perception from downstream reasoning. Used as paired supervision for text-to-audio generation, it supports semantically and temporally grounded reconstruction, together with explicit zero-shot control over event timing, speaker attributes, and word-level emphasis.

papers.title: Hierarchical Dual-Graph Retrieval for Long-form Audio Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) struggle with long-form audio reasoning, as processing entire recordings often limits to capture query-relevant content distributed across distant segments while incurring substantial computational cost. We introduce AudioHelix, a hierarchical DualGraph framework tailored for LALMs' retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. Unlike existing text-only or non-graph RAG approaches, AudioHelix connects related textual and acoustic evidence across temporally distant segments for multi-hop reasoning. Extensive experiments on TraceAV-Bench, MMAU-Pro, and AudioMarathon demonstrate that AudioHelix consistently outperforms full-audio processing and existing RAG methods. The project site is https://github.com/ewha-mmai/audiohelix.

papers.title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.

papers.title: S3-S2ST: Semantically Supervised Streaming Speech-to-Speech Translation
papers.abstract: Streaming speech-to-speech translation requires timely decisions about when partial input is sufficient for accurate translation. We present S3-S2ST, a model that learns to translate and speak from semantically aligned streaming supervision. By converting utterance-level speech pairs into incremental training examples, we teach a learned policy when to commit translations. Its adjustable threshold controls the quality--latency tradeoff on a fixed 640\,ms input grid. S3-S2ST delivers competitive English--Chinese translation on FLEURS and leads the evaluated streaming systems in translation quality on the internal 9-pair test set. On RealSI, adapting the threshold to buffered speech further improves quality over a low fixed threshold with little change in first-audio latency. We plan to release the model and code.

papers.title: MFlowAudio: Efficient Text-to-Audio Synthesis via Mamba-based Stateful Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in audio generation have been largely driven by Transformer-based diffusion models. However, these models suffer from quadratic complexity of self-attention, severely bottlenecking the long-form audio synthesis. To overcome this limitation, we propose MFlowAudio, a novel latent audio generation framework that synergizes the continuous-time dynamics of Flow Matching with a custom-designed TCMamba backbone. TCMamba uses an innovative dual-scan mechanism: a TimeMamba module to capture long-range causal dependencies with linear complexity, and a ChannelMamba module to model cross-channel correlations such as harmonic structures. Exploiting this structural foundation, we formulate the Stateful Flow Matching (SFM) paradigm. This framework inherently enables chunk-wise training and streaming generation, maintaining an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ caching complexity without incurring extra computational overhead. To enable fine-grained controllable synthesis, we devise a novel guidance mechanism that neutralizes vector field collisions precipitated by on-the-fly semantic transitions of prompts. Comprehensive empirical evaluations confirm that MFlowAudio yields generative fidelity on par with state-of-the-art baselines while establishing significant computational efficiency, achieving above $14.5$% acceleration in generation and facilitating perceptually seamless streaming synthesis with a constant latency of $1.8$ seconds. Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/mflowaudio/MFlowAudio

papers.title: Reading-Level Verification of Kanji Words in Japanese Financial Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Few-shot voice cloning makes it cheap to produce daily Japanese financial commentary with several synthetic speakers, but kanji words with more than one reading, such as the word for "market" (shijo vs. ichiba) or "overall trend" (taisei vs. oze), are still misread. A common quality gate transcribes each synthesized sentence with automatic speech recognition (ASR), converts both the input and the transcript to kana, and regenerates on mismatch. We show that this gate is unreliable in both directions: when the audio contains a misreading, the ASR language model frequently writes the expected kanji back, hiding the error, and when the audio is correct, ordinary recognition errors trigger needless regeneration. We propose a reading-level check that scores the expected reading and its confusable alternatives with a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) hiragana recognizer and flags a word when an alternative explains the audio better. On 540 utterances from three voice-cloned production voices covering 30 financial terms, with misreadings injected under controlled conditions, the transcript-based gate detected 78.9% of misreadings at a 44.4% false-alarm rate, whereas the proposed check detected 91.7% at 5.0% (AUC 0.990). On natural kanji input, it caught a front-end error that the transcript-based gate missed for one voice, and reduced regeneration requests from 38.9% to 6.1% of sentences.

papers.title: Incongruence-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition in Audio Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Voice-interactive large language models process both what a speaker says and how they say it, yet the two channels do not always agree. We ask whether that disagreement degrades speech emotion recognition. Mapping text and audio into a shared valence-arousal-dominance space, we convert the distance between them into a continuous, threshold-free incongruence score with a two-component Gaussian mixture, and validate the score against human judgement. We evaluate three audiocapable models on acted, conversational and spontaneous speech (eNTERFACE'05, MELD and CMU-MOSEI). With the model held constant across modalities, incongruence raises the odds of error whenever audio is present, in every corpus, after controlling for the ground-truth emotion and for distance in the feature space. Supervised classifiers trained on the same features behave in the opposite way, which suggests that the difficulty lies in how these models combine raw evidence rather than in the signal itself. Text-only effects are unreliable: swapping only the model that reads the transcript reverses their sign on one corpus. Rebuilding the score without the emotion lexicon reproduces the central result, and among six simpler alternatives it is the only label-free score that predicts error in all three corpora. Code, data tables and prompts are released.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Generative Models for Music Audio
papers.abstract: Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. This monograph explains the methods behind these systems for readers familiar with neural-network training who are new to music generation. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation. Worked examples connect training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. The application sections relate the musical requirements of instrumental generation, songs, editing, and live performance to model design. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information documented in papers and official sources. Symbolic composition, speech, and sound effects are included where they connect to music audio. We explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection. Selected legal decisions and disputes illustrate the implications for training and release. The reviewed systems combine established generative paradigms with new representations, planning stages, and post-training procedures. Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: music generation, audio generation, neural audio codec

papers.title: AudioRSI: Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

papers.title: Pronunciation-Supervised Text-to-Speech for Irish (Gaeilge)
papers.abstract: Speech technology for Irish must be built from very little transcribed speech, yet the language's pronunciation is thoroughly documented in dictionaries and dialect descriptions. We ask whether that documentation can supervise the adaptation of a large pretrained text-to-speech model to a language it was never trained on. We adapt Qwen3-TTS to Irish using 12.8 hours of crowdsourced Common Voice speech, correcting two defects in the vendor fine-tuning script that training loss does not reveal (Appendix A), and reach character error rate (CER) 0.225 on held-out cross-corpus text, against 0.397 for an exhaustively tuned from-scratch system and 0.437 for zero-shot cloning. We then compile the Wiktionary pronunciation record into a lexicon and a phoneme critic, and use that critic as the verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning: CER 0.159 cross-corpus and 0.067 in-domain, with the voice still anonymous across all 202 training speakers. The same critic explains why the voice cannot yet be steered to a minority dialect: 229 of 12,311 training clips lean Ulster against 8,451 Munster. Pronunciation documentation, converted into a verifier, is a practical lever for low-resource speech synthesis, and a way to measure what the available data cannot support.

papers.title: DRC-TTS: A Dual-Resolution Codec-Based Architecture for Lexicon-Free Malay Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Modern discrete neural audio codecs facilitate speech synthesis by replacing continuous acoustic representations with low-frame-rate discrete token sequences. For Malay speech synthesis, character-level input reduces reliance on pronunciation lexicons. However, combining character-level inputs with low-frame-rate discrete codecs introduces a temporal alignment challenge. When predicted character durations are quantized into frame counts at 12.5 Hz, durations shorter than one codec frame may be assigned zero frames. Consequently, the corresponding character representations may be lost during length regulation, potentially leading to pronunciation omissions. This study proposes DRC-TTS, a dual-resolution codec-based architecture for lexicon-free Malay speech synthesis. The model expands character representations at a temporal resolution of 50 Hz and subsequently downsamples them through strided convolution to 12.5 Hz for discrete codec-token prediction. Objective evaluations show that the proposed model reduces the character error rate (CER) from 27.11% for the baseline to 21.86%, an absolute reduction of 5.25 percentage points. The proposed model also achieves a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.30, compared with 4.12 for the baseline. These results suggest that the dual-resolution design may improve character-level alignment and perceived speech naturalness under the evaluated conditions.

papers.title: MixCards: Evaluating Structured Descriptions of Multi-Source Sound Scenes
papers.abstract: Audio captioning benchmarks typically evaluate a single unstructured free-text description of an audio scene, providing limited insight into how a model fails to understand polyphonic audio. A plausible caption may omit a source, or conflate multiple sources into one, or assign an attribute of one source to another, and conventional captioning evaluation cannot locate these errors. We introduce MixCardBench, a benchmark for structured captioning of polyphonic audio, which evaluates models in two stages: first, identifying and temporally localizing the sources in a scene, and second, generating a structured MixCard describing the semantic, temporal, and acoustic properties of each source. The benchmark contains 4884 ecologically plausible synthetic soundscapes with up to nine overlapping speech, music and sound effects sources built from high-quality recordings and source-level annotations, where each source has a reference MixCard. We evaluate six state-of-the-art large audio language models and find substantial limitations in current models, which struggle considerably with speech and sound effects timing and detection, with the strongest model reaching only around 60% mean card-field score. Performance varies significantly across attributes, exposing capability differences that are hidden by aggregate caption scores. We assess the quality and ecological validity of MixCardBench through human validation, distribution matching and a listening study, and show that human corrections have little effect on model rankings, and our synthesized soundscapes are closer to in-the-wild YouTube videos than source guided but otherwise random synthesis. The benchmark dataset and code are publicly available, and demo examples are at https://mixcards-anon.github.io/mixcards-demo/

papers.title: StreamSE: Neural Audio Codec-based Streaming Speech Enhancement for On-device Inference
papers.abstract: Recent generative speech enhancement (SE) models achieve high perceptual quality, but their non-causal processing and expensive computation make them difficult to use for streaming, on-device inference. We propose StreamSE, a 20M-parameter streaming SE model that operates in the latent space of a frozen pretrained neural audio codec. At each frame, StreamSE directly regresses a clean continuous latent from the noisy continuous latent while conditioning on its own predictions from previous frames. Enhancement therefore requires a single forward pass per frame and no iterative sampling or look-ahead. We further truncate the codec's residual vector quantizer (RVQ) to its coarse levels, halving the number of tokens per frame while improving robustness to reverberation. StreamSE is the only streaming generative model in our comparison, yet it matches or exceeds the perceptual quality of the offline generative baselines. Furthermore, the complete StreamSE pipeline runs in real time on a single smartphone CPU core. Our results show that continuous latent regression provides a practical route to generative SE under fully causal, on-device streaming constraints.

papers.title: Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
papers.abstract: Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.

papers.title: Beyond Utterance-Level Speaker Similarity: Perception-Aligned Segmental Evaluation of Accent in Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech. We introduce a segmental evaluation protocol combining speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword annotations of perceived accent differences provided by listeners from target accent regions. Using newly collected recordings, 47 retained listeners evaluate 200 content-matched reference--candidate pairs spanning four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems, and an articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes yield different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated ($ρ= 0.71$), highlighting the value of examining local perceptual evidence beyond these scores. Evaluation of seven objective distances reveals weak correspondence with subword selections, with correlations reaching at most $ρ= 0.22$. We release code, data, and an interactive demo to support the development of perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.

papers.title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
papers.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

papers.title: Nedimo: An Evidence-Grounded Multilingual Pipeline for AI-Generated Sleep Stories
papers.abstract: Generative audio systems can produce large libraries of personalized bedtime content, but ordinary media objectives (retention, completion, and novelty) are poorly aligned with the goal of supporting a transition toward sleep. Direct evidence for narrated bedtime audio in adults is mixed, and a recent active-controlled trial did not support such audio as a standalone treatment for sleep disturbance. We translate this uncertain evidence into conservative engineering requirements and present a multilingual pipeline for generating and narrating low-arousal sleep stories. The implemented prototype separates deterministic planning from large language model generation, represents content and delivery parameters explicitly, shapes each script through a four-phase attention taper, validates structural and lexical constraints, performs a bounded error-aware retry, and quarantines unresolved outputs. Provider-agnostic text-to-speech synthesis is followed by paragraph-aware joining, two-pass loudness normalization, and a publication gate that re-measures the saved, encoded file against fixed loudness, loudness-range, and true-peak limits. The product data model records stop position, replay, early abandonment, and completion while treating these events as ambiguous behavioral proxies rather than clinical outcomes. We contribute an evidence-to-requirement mapping, a traceable guardrail architecture with explicit acceptance thresholds, technical evaluation criteria, and a prospective protocol for testing sleep-onset effects. No clinical efficacy is claimed; the system is positioned as a relaxation and attentional-support tool whose benefit and possible reliance must be evaluated empirically.

papers.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
papers.abstract: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Transformer Encoders for Audio-Image-Symbolic Music Retrieval
papers.abstract: Score-based multimodal music retrieval requires representations that are both discriminative within each modality and compatible across audio recordings, sheet music images, and symbolic scores. This paper investigates the effectiveness of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for adapting pretrained music encoders and examines whether modality-specific improvements translate into better multimodal representations. We compare full fine-tuning, LoRA, and QLoRA across nine pretrained audio, image, and symbolic score encoders on TriScore and the Musical Theme Dataset. Encoders are first evaluated and selected through supervised unimodal classification, using frozen-encoder linear probing as a reference. We then introduce a controlled 2x2 design crossing encoder adaptation with task-specific shared projection, comparing frozen and adapted representations before and after projection. LoRA or QLoRA is selected in 14 of 18 modality-target combinations, frequently matching or outperforming full fine-tuning while optimizing substantially fewer parameters. However, these unimodal gains do not transfer uniformly to multimodal classification. Adaptation and projection are complementary for composer classification on TriScore, largely redundant for TriScore instrument and the Musical Theme Dataset instrument and ensemble tasks, and partially interfering for composer classification on the Musical Theme Dataset. The final adapted-and-projected title representation on TriScore supports piece-level retrieval, reaching average Top-5 and Top-10 accuracies of 55.32 and 64.68, respectively. Cross-modal exclusion and neighborhood analyses further reveal strong modality-specific local structure in the projected spaces. Overall, PEFT provides an effective and computationally efficient alternative to full fine-tuning, but improved unimodal discrimination alone does not guarantee better multimodal organization.

papers.title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use
papers.abstract: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $τ$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

papers.title: Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
papers.abstract: The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.

papers.title: SpeakerTurn: Target-Speaker Semantic Turn Detection in Multi-Speaker Environments
papers.abstract: Semantic completeness alone cannot determine when an assistant should respond in a multi-speaker environment: a completed utterance may belong to an interfering speaker, while the designated user is still speaking, acknowledging, or requesting time. We therefore study semantic turn inference conditioned on speaker identity. We propose SpeakerTurn, a framework that jointly predicts the target transcript and turn state from a speech mixture and an independent target-speaker reference. Built on CocktailASR-1, it links semantic decisions to the corresponding target content through joint supervision, distinguishing complete, incomplete, backchannel, wait, and target-absent states, with a separate interruption task. We also examine whether structured chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision improves decisions by representing speaker presence and semantic cues. On a synthetic multi-speaker test set, SpeakerTurn achieves five-state macro F1 of 0.811 and target-transcription character error rate (CER) of 4.20%, correctly resolving all ten reference-swapped interruption pairs. Joint-format transcription and native-interface recognition nevertheless behave differently, and CoT improves validation transcription without improving turn macro F1. These results show why target attribution, semantic turn discrimination, and recognition retention require separate assessment when adapting speech language models for speaker-conditioned interaction.

papers.title: SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
papers.abstract: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

## Model Description

**Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0** is an audio-capable version of [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1).
The model was developed by [LINAGORA](https://linagora.com) and
the [OpenLLM-France](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France) consortium, as part of the OpenLLM France project funded by
[BPI France](https://www.bpifrance.fr/) under the France 2030 program.

The training of Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 was conducted on the Jean Zay supercomputer managed by [IDRIS](http://www.idris.fr/docs/idris/missions),
using the [NVIDIA NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) toolkit.
The model was trained on various tasks and types of audio, including ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), AST (Automatic Speech Translation), QA (Question Answering), Sound (Question Answering and Captioning), Music (Question Answering and Captioning) and more.

### Bias, Risks, and Limitations

- Inherits the limitations of the base [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1)
  language model: it can struggle with math word problems and is susceptible to hallucination.
- Training sequences were capped at 16,384 tokens (audio and text combined), so longer contexts are untested.
<!-- - The audio encoder and its front-end were entirely frozen during training, so audio understanding is bounded by what
  Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 already hears: the model cannot learn to compensate for acoustic conditions the
  encoder itself handles poorly. -->
- Language coverage is uneven. French and English make up most of the training mix and are the only languages seen on every task. German, Spanish and Italian were seen in training for ASR, AST and spoken QA. Portuguese, Dutch and Arabic for ASR and AST only.
- Arabic is the weakest language: the frozen Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 encoder was not trained on Arabic,
  so the model is clearly less reliable there (FLEURS WER ~30%).
<!-- - LoRA fine-tuning only touches attention projections in the LLM; no additional audio-specific safety or
  refusal tuning was performed beyond what the base LLM already has. -->

### Recommendations

- Speech, sound and music understanding (summarization, captioning, sound/music QA, conversation):
  best in French and English, the only languages the model was trained on for these tasks.
- Transcription (ASR) and translation (AST): supported in French, English, German, Spanish,
  Italian, Portuguese and Dutch. For production ASR/AST pipelines, a dedicated model may still
  perform better.
- Spoken question answering: mainly supported in French and English. German, Spanish and
  Italian are also supported, but with far less training data.
- Other languages and tasks: outside French and English, evaluate the model on your own data
  before relying on it, especially for a task the model was not trained on in that language.
- Up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge: as with the base LLM, pair the model with a RAG
  pipeline.

## Training details

### Training data

Trained on the [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset),
a large multilingual, multi-task collection of audio–text conversations comprising: ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition),
AST (Automatic Speech Translation), spoken question answering, summarization, diarization, temporal localization,
speaker/gender/age/emotion/language recognition, and music/sound captioning and QA (Question Answering).

### Instruction template

Same chat template as the base LLM (inspired by Qwen3), extended with an `<|audio|>` locator tag:
wherever `<|audio|>` appears in a turn, the corresponding audio segment is encoded and its embeddings
replace the tag before the sequence reaches the LLM. Conversations can carry several audio clips and mix
audio-only, text-only, and audio+text turns within the same dialogue (see the
[dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset) for example
conversations).

### Training Procedure

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| **Audio encoder** | [Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3) Conformer encoder, frozen |
| **RoTE** | Applied between audio encoder and audio adapter. θ=1200, rotary fraction=0.2. Inspired by [Goel et al., 2024, OMCAT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12109).|
| **Audio adapter** | Linear projection into the LLM embedding space (1024 -> 4096) |
| **LLM** | [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1), adapted with LoRA (on `q_proj`/`v_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, r=64, α=64) |
| **Trainable params** | 82.1M / ~8.2B (1.0%) |
| **Optimizer** | AdamW (β=(0.9, 0.98), weight decay 0.001) |
| **LR schedule** | Cosine annealing (max LR 2e-4, min LR 1e-6, 500 warmup steps) |
| **Batching** | Dynamic, bucketed by audio duration (27 buckets) |
| **Steps** | 100,000 |
| **Gradient clipping** | 1.0 |
| **Strategy** | FSDP2 (full sharding), activation checkpointing on the LLM (to allow for long sequences), 1 node × 4 H100 |
| **Precision** | bf16 |

The model was trained for 100k steps and drew from a weighted, randomly-ordered, sharded mix of that dataset,
bucketed by duration into 27 buckets (up to 1,200s / 16,384 audio-equivalent tokens per example) with a
matching dynamic batch size per bucket (238 down to 1).

Validation covered CommonVoice ASR (fr/en/ar),
Multilingual TEDx speech translation (fr→en), spoken QA (SLUE-SQA-5, VoxPopuli-QA, en/fr), and audio/music
captioning (AudioCaps, MusicCaps).

The training code and configs are available in the [Luciole-Audio-Training repository](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training). Training used an updated version of [NeMo/Speech 3.1](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) which can be found in our [NeMo/Speech fork](https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo/tree/luciole_speech.3.1.0-rc0).

## Evaluation

To evaluate our models and compare them with other open-weight Audio LLMs, we used [our fork of AudioBench](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/AudioBench). We used a combination of datasets from AudioBench and datasets available in [our HF audio evaluation repository](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Evaluation-Dataset). You can find the full details and results on [our AudioBench leaderboard](https://openllm-france.github.io/AudioBench/).

A small excerpt from the leaderboard, showing the main table across all tasks and languages:

![results.png](assets/results.png)

Results for French and English only, as well as for ASR, AST, and QA tasks only:

![results_fr_en.png](assets/results_fr_en.png)

As you can see, the model [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0) performs well in French and English compared to other models.

For more detailed results in French ASR you can take a look at our [🏆 French ASR Leaderboard](https://linagora-labs.github.io/asr_benchmark/) where we use various types of datasets to evaluate the open source models. 


## Using the model

### With vLLM

The exported checkpoint's `config.json` declares `"model_type": "nemo_speechlm"` and
`"architectures": ["NeMoSpeechLMForConditionalGeneration"]`. Both are registered with vLLM by the SALM
plugin that ships inside `nemo-toolkit`
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/tree/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/vllm/salm))
via the `vllm.general_plugins` entry point:

```toml
[project.entry-points."vllm.general_plugins"]
nemo_speechlm = "nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm:register"
```

vLLM auto-discovers this plugin at startup as soon as `nemo-toolkit` and `vllm` are installed in the same
environment. The plugin merges the
LoRA adapters into the LLM backbone on load and runs the frozen Parakeet encoder + connector to turn each
`<|audio|>` tag into the right number of audio-embedding slots before generation.

**Install using uv**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
uv pip install vllm==0.28.0
uv pip install "numpy<=2.4"
```

**Serve**

```bash
vllm serve OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 \
    --max-model-len 16384
```

**Query** (OpenAI-compatible chat API, audio sent as base64):

```python
import base64
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")

with open("sample.wav", "rb") as f:   # 16 kHz mono
    audio_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Transcris cet audio en français : <|audio|>"},
                {"type": "input_audio", "input_audio": {"data": audio_b64, "format": "wav"}},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

The `<|audio|>` placeholder is the same `audio_locator_tag` used during training: put it in the text
wherever the audio should be attended to; the plugin expands it automatically. Audio must be 16 kHz mono;
the encoder supports chunked processing for long-form audio (well beyond the durations seen in training).

### With NeMo

The checkpoint can also be loaded directly with NeMo's `SALM` class
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.models.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/models/salm.py)).

**Install**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
```

**Load and generate:**

```python
import torch
from nemo.collections.speechlm2 import SALM

model = SALM.from_pretrained("OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0")  # or a local checkpoint directory
model = model.eval().to(torch.bfloat16).to("cuda")

# High-level API: pass the audio file path(s) directly in the prompt, next to the
# `<|audio|>` placeholder; SALM loads and resamples the audio for you.
answer_ids = model.generate(
    prompts=[
        [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Transcris cet audio en français : {model.audio_locator_tag}",
                "audio": ["sample.wav"],
            }
        ]
    ],
    max_new_tokens=256,
)
print(model.tokenizer.ids_to_text(answer_ids[0].tolist()))
```

A prompt can carry several turns and several audio clips (one `<|audio|>` tag per clip, in order).

### Example prompts for each task

- ASR: 
  - English: `Make a word-for-word transcription in English of the spoken content.`
  - French: `Fais une transcription mot pour mot en français du contenu parlé.`
  - German: `Erstelle eine wortwörtliche Transkription des gesprochenen Inhalts auf Deutsch.`
  - Spanish: `Haz una transcripción palabra por palabra en español del contenido hablado.`
  - Italian: `Fai una trascrizione parola per parola in italiano del contenuto parlato.`
  - Portuguese: `Faça uma transcrição palavra por palavra em português do conteúdo falado.`
  - Dutch: `Maak een woord-voor-woord transcriptie in het Nederlands van de gesproken inhoud.`
  - No language given: `Can you write the text of this audio file in its source language?`
- QA: `Listen to the audio and answer the question.`
- AST: `Translate this file into French.`
- Diarization: 
  - `Provide a time-stamped, speaker-attributed transcript of this audio.`
  - `Transcris et diarise cet enregistrement, avec les horodatages de chaque tour.`

Ming-3.0-audio-flash

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash is a native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤖 ModelScope · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 126B total parameters, 6.5B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-flash combines an audio encoder and projector with a Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output.

## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --voice US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference 128K serving profile uses tensor parallelism across four 80 GB H800 GPUs. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only or Talker output. On particularly long audio inputs, the four-GPU profiles may OOM; in that case, switch to the corresponding eight-GPU fallback profile (`deploy/*_8gpu.yaml`), which sets `tensor_parallel_size: 8` across GPUs 0–7 (and the Talker reuses GPU 7). See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. For speech output, start the audio profile and select an IP or registered voice with the vLLM-Omni client's `--voice` option: ```bash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" python examples/vllm_omni_audio_chat.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --audio-response \ --voice US_Stella \ --output-audio outputs/answer.wav ``` The client sends this selection as Chat Completions `audio.voice: {"id": "..."}`. vLLM-Omni uses the built-in IP voice `灵小柔` when no voice is specified. The model directory also provides `灵楷` and `US_James` as preset reference voices under `voice_presets/voice_audio/`, with their matching transcripts in `voice_presets/voice_prompts.json`. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated SGLang profile uses four GPUs and provides text output. See the [SGLang example](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/examples/sglang_audio_chat.py) for client usage. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/) serves transcription, audio chat, and speech synthesis from one server. Serving uses two GPUs: `--thinker.tp_size 2` places the thinker on both visible devices, the audio encoder uses GPU 0, and speech synthesis uses GPU 1. ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 sgl-omni serve \ --model-path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --thinker.tp_size 2 ``` The server exposes OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/speech`, and `/v1/chat/completions` endpoints. See the [SGLang-Omni cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/ming3_audio.html) for client examples, including voice cloning with `ref_audio` and `ref_text`. ## Evaluation ### Speech Recognition

# YuE2-3B · MLX 4-bit

[YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) quantized to 4-bit for
[MLX](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx). It turns lyrics and a style prompt
into a full song, vocals and accompaniment, on Apple silicon, including iPhone.

All the weights together take **2.15 GB**. The two transformer models shrink from 7.2 GB in bf16 to 2.0 GB. A 30-second song
generates in **82 seconds on an iPhone 17 Pro Max** running iOS 26.6.

Published by [Milliwatt Labs](https://milliwattlabs.com). This is an unofficial
conversion. For the model itself, its training and its benchmarks, see the
[original model card](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B).

## Samples

Generated on a Mac mini (M4) with this 4-bit model. More on [EM Radio](https://radio.transistorkit.com/), streaming 24/7.

| Song | Artist | Genre | Listen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Better Off | Kira Nova | Pop | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/better-off.m4a"></audio> |
| Signal | Ada Ray | Top 40 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/signal.m4a"></audio> |
| Coal Miner's Blood | Boone Harlan | Country | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/coal-miners-blood.m4a"></audio> |

| Pressure | Blaze Meridian | Hip-hop | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/resolve/main/samples/pressure.m4a"></audio> |

## Apps

Free apps built on this model. [ChorusPop](https://choruspop.com) adds stems, MIDI import and export, and an instrumental mode.

| Platform | App |
|---|---|
| iPhone and iPad | [ChorusPop (TestFlight beta)](https://testflight.apple.com/join/b7j7z3CT) |
| Mac | [ChorusPop for Mac (zip)](https://choruspop.com/download/ChorusPop-1.0.zip) |
| Android | [ChorusPop for Android (APK beta)](https://choruspop.com/beta/ChorusPop-android.apk). Uses YuE2 weights converted for Android, not these MLX files. |

## Files

| Directory | What | Precision | Size |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `weights/ar-4bit/` | Autoregressive LM (Qwen3 architecture, 28 layers). Writes the ABC score, then the audio codec tokens. | 4-bit, group size 64 | 1.22 GB |
| `weights/nar-4bit/` | Non-autoregressive velocity model. Turns codec tokens into audio latents. | 4-bit, group size 64; latent interface (`llm2vae`, `vae2llm`, `time_embedder`) kept in bf16 | 0.80 GB |
| `weights/vae-decoder/` | Oobleck decoder from [YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae). Turns 25 Hz latents into 48 kHz stereo audio. | fp16 | 0.13 GB |

Also in `weights/`: the tokenizer (`qwen.tiktoken`) and the sampling settings
(`yue2_generation_config.json`). At the repo root: the MLX runner (`yue2_mlx.py`,
`run_song.py`), `requirements.txt`, and the license files.

Quantization is MLX's affine `mx.quantize` (4 bits, group size 64). The AR
directory is a standard `qwen3` MLX checkpoint with a `quantization` block in
`config.json`.

## Changes from the original

As the CC BY-NC 4.0 license requires, here is what was changed:

- The AR and NAR linear weights are quantized to 4-bit (affine, group size 64).
  Norms and the NAR latent interface stay in bf16.
- In the VAE decoder, weight normalization is folded into plain weights
  (`g · v / ‖v‖`), stored in fp16. Only the decoder is included.
- The tensors were rearranged into three MLX checkpoints. No weights were
  retrained or fine-tuned.

## Quality compared with bf16

Each number compares this conversion with the original bf16 weights on the
same prompt and seed. That's one song, so treat it as a fidelity check, not a
benchmark.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| AR codec tokens: top-1 agreement with bf16 (teacher-forced) | 82.9% |
| AR codec KL divergence from bf16 | 0.023 |
| AR codec perplexity, 4-bit / bf16 | 39.3 / 40.0 |
| AR score (ABC) tokens: top-1 agreement | 98.8% |
| NAR velocity cosine vs bf16 | 0.9965 |
| Rendered latents, cosine vs bf16 (same codec tokens and noise) | 0.985 |
| VAE decoder fp16 vs fp32 | 60.8 dB SNR |
| Free-running song from lyrics | Finishes normally (emits the end-of-music token), 560 score + 1,056 codec tokens |

For the same seed, the 4-bit model doesn't reproduce the bf16 song note for
note. Its songs drift into a different, equally valid performance.

## On a Mac

One full song, measured on a Mac mini (M4, 16 GB) running macOS 26.5 with
MLX 0.32.2. The model ended the song on its own after 61.9 seconds of audio.

| Stage | Seconds |
|---|---:|
| Load (tokenizer, AR, NAR) | 1.7 |
| Score (ABC), 691 tokens at 80 tokens/s | 9.6 |
| Codec tokens, 1,548 at 85 tokens/s | 19.0 |
| NAR (codec → latents), 32 steps | 116.1 |
| VAE decode | 5.2 |
| **Total** | **152** |

Peak MLX memory was 3.5 GB, during VAE decode.

## On iPhone

A 30-second clip, measured on an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 26.6:

| Stage | Seconds |
|---|---:|
| Load (tokenizer, AR) | 0.6 |
| Score (ABC), 26 tokens/s | 23.2 |
| Codec tokens (750), 41 tokens/s | 18.8 |
| NAR (codec → latents) | 34.3 |
| VAE decode | 4.3 |
| **Total** | **81.6** |

- **Memory:** peak footprint 1.9 GB during generation and 3.6 GB during VAE decode.
- **Thermal state:** nominal the whole run.
- **Latents** match the reference implementation's latents at cosine 0.9995 for
  the same tokens.

## Usage

**Requirements**

- An Apple silicon Mac (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
- 8 GB of memory minimum; 16 GB recommended. A 3½-minute song peaks at 3.5 GB.
- macOS 14 or later.
- Python 3.10 or later.

Tested on a Mac mini (M4, 16 GB) with macOS 26, Python 3.12, `mlx` 0.32.2
and `mlx-lm` 0.29.1.

Got it running on another Mac? Let us know in the
[Community](https://huggingface.co/milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit/discussions)
tab which Mac it was and how long a song took.

```bash
pip install mlx mlx-lm numpy tiktoken huggingface_hub
hf download milliwattlabs/YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit --local-dir YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit
cd YuE2-3B-MLX-4bit

python run_song.py --weights weights --out out \
  --style "upbeat indie pop, warm female lead vocal, acoustic guitar, light drums" \
  --lyrics "$(cat lyrics.txt)" --seed 11
```

The song is written to `out/song.wav` (48 kHz stereo), and the score to
`out/abc.txt`. Lyrics use `[verse]` and `[chorus]` section tags. The same seed
gives a different song than the original PyTorch release, because MLX uses a
different random number generator.

`--cot` picks how much of the score the model writes before the audio:
`full` (melody and chords, the default), `melody`, or `off`.

## Limitations

- **Non-commercial only.** The license comes from the original weights (see below).
- Everything in the original card's limitations applies here too.
- The runner generates a song in a single context window. Songs longer than
  one window, which the original splits into chunks, aren't supported yet.
- The quality figures above cover one prompt and one seed. Listen before relying on it.
- Only the decoder half of the VAE is included, so this conversion can't
  encode reference audio. Cover mode, which needs the encoder, isn't supported.

# YuE2 Turbo — Intel Arc B70 + NVIDIA RTX 4080

**Measured real-time music generation with YuE2 3B, now including Apollo's RTX 4080 CUDA port.**
This repository now contains the **actual Q8_0 model, F16 VAE, tokenizer and config files**,
plus the optimized source/runtime release and listening gallery. It is **not a new fine-tune**.
It uses [m-a-p/YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) via
[audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF) and
[audio.cpp](https://github.com/JarodMica/audio.cpp). The exact benchmarked model files are hosted here, unchanged from the attributed upstream GGUF release.

## Download the actual model

**The model is hosted in this repository—not just linked elsewhere.**
The model bundle is **4.53 GB total** (decimal), including the exact files used in the published benchmarks:

| YuE2 3B Q8_0 | [Actual GGUF weights](https://huggingface.co/Frosty40/YuE2-B70-Turbo/resolve/main/models/Yue2-3B-GGUF/yue2-3b-q8_0.gguf?download=true) | 4.264 GB |
| YuE2 F16 VAE | [Actual VAE weights](https://huggingface.co/Frosty40/YuE2-B70-Turbo/resolve/main/models/Yue2-3B-GGUF/yue2-vae-f16.gguf?download=true) | 265.2 MB |

[Build/run instructions](apollo/BUILD-AND-RUN.md).
Weights are the unchanged audio-cpp conversion of m-a-p/YuE2-3B—not an original fine-tune.
The measured speedups require the included optimized runtime; copying the weights alone does not accelerate stock software.

## Listen: Knight Shift Radio

### [Tune in to Knight Shift Radio →](https://knight-shift-radio.vercel.app/)

Original YuE2 music, with warm Kasey song introductions and separate Jessica tech/AI information segments.
The show's direction is developed arrangements, thoughtful genre transitions and positive lyrics about
kindness, hard work and shared progress. Speech uses ElevenLabs separately from YuE2 music.
The public site is linked here; stream availability and the live rundown can change.
No claim is made that the samples below are currently scheduled or on air.

## Latest measured results — Apollo RTX 4080, 2026-11-02

RTX 4080 16 GB; CUDA 13.0, SM 8.9; Q8_0 YuE2-3B + F16 VAE. GPU clocks and power limits unchanged.
One warmup discarded, then **three separate measured cold CLI processes** per full-song configuration.
Speed is audio seconds / elapsed seconds. Session and startup-inclusive numbers are deliberately separate.

| Workload | NAR steps | Audio | Median session speed | Median including CLI startup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| city_lights, cache-off baseline | 8 | 69.00 s | 3.173× | 3.030× |
| city_lights, accepted full-song runtime | 8 | 69.00 s | **3.168×** | **3.019×** |
| Same accepted runtime | 32 | 69.00 s | **2.754×** | **2.648×** |
| Four-minute song | 8 | 257.08 s | **3.322×** | **3.269×** |

In practical terms, the 4:17 song takes about **79 seconds including CLI startup**.
At 32 steps, city_lights takes about **26 seconds including startup** for 69 seconds of audio.
The cache-on/off difference is within noise; **no CUDA prefix-cache speedup is claimed**.
Long-song NAR takes 10.09–10.19 s versus about 3.8–4.0 s on the short song: no superlinear
penalty was observed at the measured window size. This is not a universal scaling law.

- [Short-song runs](apollo/receipts/city-lights-results.json) · [Long-song runs](apollo/receipts/long-song-results.json)
- [Acceptance summary](apollo/ACCEPTANCE.json) · [Full results and rejected experiments](apollo/RESULTS.md)
- [Build/reconstruction instructions](apollo/BUILD-AND-RUN.md) · [Source/runtime manifests](apollo/RELEASE.json)

### Streaming: first audio in 8.56–9.43 seconds, 3/3 passed

The adapter-safe asynchronous NAR preload runtime produces first audio **including cold CLI startup** at
**8.555, 9.165 and 9.432 seconds**. Each run naturally completes **256.839 s** of stereo PCM in
21 contiguous chunks, with **zero late chunks and zero gaps**. Its PCM is byte-identical to the original
streaming predecessor for this exact request. This does not claim bit parity between CUDA and SYCL,
model-quality parity, or tested LoRA output parity (adapter sources fall back to the ordinary loader).

The original, pinned-upload, retained-mapping and earlier-score variants that missed the latency gate
remain in the receipts. They are not promoted or silently hidden.
[All three accepted runs](apollo/receipts/stream-preload-v3-results.json) ·
[Accepted streaming identity](apollo/receipts/accepted-stream-artifact.json).

### Thirty-minute playlist: passed

**1,800 seconds of real-paced PCM consumption**, 86,400,000 stereo frames, zero queue failures,
zero fallback items and zero inserted-silence frames; expected/actual PCM SHA256 match.
This is an isolated producer/consumer soak, **not** a network-stream or physical-audio-device test,
and does not establish listener delivery or perfect musical transitions.
[Playlist receipt](apollo/receipts/playlist-soak-final-results.json).

The arrangements request evolving sections, instrumental interplay and a natural ending.

## B70 results and research — history retained, latest recheck disclosed

The previously published November 1 B70 measurements remain available:
**3.091× session realtime** on city_lights at 8 steps, **2.414×** at 32 steps,
**2.141×** on Knight Won't Stop at 32 steps, first streaming audio **7.58–7.73 s**,
and a passing 30-minute isolated queue. [Previous card and linked receipts](history/README-before-apollo-20261102.md).

The **November 2 canonical B70 recheck failed the 3.0× gate**, median **2.818×**
(2.818, 2.141, 2.939×). All three songs naturally completed and exceeded 55 seconds.
This does not erase the earlier pass and is not an Apollo result.
[Latest B70 recheck receipt](apollo/receipts/b70-required-recheck-results.json).
No new B70 GPU execution was performed for this publication.

Recent research/audits cover native sampler behavior, seed contract, generation defaults,
Q8/F16 cache and PCM rail accounting, VAE tiling, decoder precision and official-decoder comparisons.
These are **scoped experimental or diagnostic findings**, not all production improvements or end-to-end speedups.
[Research index](research/README.md) · [Evidence reconciliation](research/EVIDENCE-REVIEW-20261101.md).
The historical October recipe, charts and earlier songs remain in this repository;
[read the prior card](history/README-before-apollo-20261102.md) for that material.

## What changed on Apollo

The CUDA port carries over growing AR buffers, cached NAR prefixes, bounded NAR windows
(1024 frames / 128 overlap), and deferred packed-weight uploads from the B70 work.
CUDA Flash Attention and CUDA graphs replace Intel-specific kernels. An independent, opt-in streaming
pipeline overlaps safe NAR weight loading with earlier work and preserves the tested predecessor PCM.
The measured full-song runtime stays frozen; streaming has its own binary and source identity.
The older engine ignores `yue2.packed_projections` and `yue2.kv_cache_alignment` request keys:
they are retained where present in raw historical receipts, but receive no performance credit.

## Reproduce / download

Start with [Apollo build and run instructions](apollo/BUILD-AND-RUN.md).
The pinned source base, patches, source archive SHA256, accepted executable SHA256s,
model hashes and protocol receipts are included. Linux x86-64 CUDA executables are provided
as **experimental, hardware/environment-specific artifacts**, not a portable installer.
Rebuilding is supported by the recorded source recipe, but byte-identical rebuilds are not claimed.
Download the model and runtime together from this repo; the model remains **CC BY-NC 4.0**. Nothing in this release changes your radio queue.

## Limitations, attribution and licenses

These are local measured results, not official benchmark/leaderboard scores or a world-record claim.
No official-model waveform/quality parity is established. Cross-hardware sampled trajectories can differ.
Signal checks are not listening approval: some takes have PCM rail samples and naturally quiet tails.
The queue test does not certify internet delivery, actual loudspeaker output, host cadence or genre transitions.

- audio.cpp: ShugoAI LLC, **Apache-2.0**. Its bundled third-party components retain their licenses;
  the source archive includes those notices. SYCL EXPM1/concat work derives from ggml/llama.cpp (**MIT**).
- Project engine patches and scripts: Apache-2.0; model card, charts and generated music: CC BY-NC 4.0.
- The previous card preserves the detailed contributor/tool credits and historical release narrative.
  [NOTICE](NOTICE) records the existing licensing credits. Not affiliated with or endorsed by m-a-p,
  ShugoAI, NVIDIA, Intel, or the ggml authors.

--- license: cc-by-4.0 language: - hi - te - en library_name: moshi pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio base_model: kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16 tags: - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - spoken-dialogue - moshi - hindi - telugu - indic --- # siba · full-duplex speech for Hindi, Telugu and English **siba** is a speech-to-speech dialogue model that listens and speaks at the same time, built by adapting Kyutai's [Moshi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16) to Hindi and Telugu while keeping English. This repository holds the current **Stage 2b** checkpoint plus the Stage 1 base checkpoints it was built from. | | | |---|---| | **Model** | Moshiko (~7.7B parameters, Mimi codec) with a 48k text vocabulary (+16k Hindi/Telugu pieces) | | **Languages** | Hindi, Telugu, English | | **Training** | Stage 1: ~33k h YouTube monologue speech → Stage 2b: 517 h two-channel dialogues, 1,500 steps | | **Agent voices** | one fixed voice per language (Hindi: Ritvik) | | **Status** | research checkpoint — turn-taking works, answer relevance and response speed do not yet | | **Weights** | [`stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/consolidated.safetensors`](stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated) (15.7 GB, bf16) | ## Highlights - **Listens before it speaks.** In Full-Duplex-Bench v1 it stays quiet through 78–81% of the user's mid-sentence pauses, where the original Moshi talks over every one, and it talks over the user in 25% of cases versus 89%. - **Right language, right role.** After dialogue training it replies in the language of the conversation and as an assistant; the Stage 1 model before it monologues, often in the wrong language. - **Still slow and often off-topic.** It takes 1.4–2 s to respond and often does not answer what was asked, especially in Hindi and Telugu (see [Limitations](#limitations)). ## Results ### Full-Duplex-Bench v1 (English) ![Full-Duplex-Bench v1 components, siba Stage 2b vs the original Moshiko](stage2b/assets/fdb_v1.png) | | siba Stage 2b | Moshiko | |---|:---:|:---:| | **Duplex score** (0–100) | **38.4** | **54.5** | | Talks over the user in mid-sentence pauses ↓ | **0.19 – 0.22** | 1.00 | | Talk-over share of all cases ↓ | **0.25** | 0.89 | | Takes the turn when the user finishes ↑ | 0.92 | 1.00 | | Latency to take the turn ↓ | 1.36 s | 0.00 s* | | Yields when interrupted ↑ / latency ↓ | 0.94 / 2.00 s | 0.92 / 0.68 s | | Backchannel frequency ↑ | 0.06 | 0.16 | 25% subset: the first 36 samples of each of the 5 tasks (180), both models run with the same streaming inference. The duplex score is a timing-only composite of the four components (each takes the takeover rate and gives full latency credit at ≤0.3 s, none at ≥2 s); the official GPT relevance judge was not run. \*Moshi's 0 s latency means it was already talking — its higher score partly rewards that. ### Held-out loss ![Held-out first-codebook loss by language during Stage 2b](stage2b/assets/heldout_loss.png) | Step | Hindi | Telugu | English | |---|:---:|:---:|:---:| | 0 (Stage 1, before dialogue training) | 7.94 | 7.69 | 7.71 | | 500 | 0.835 | 0.925 | 0.572 | | **1500 (released)** | **0.807** | **0.904** | **0.562** | 48 held-out one-minute units per language. No overfitting: the final step is the best. ## Quick start ```bash pip install moshi huggingface_hub ``` ```python import torch from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download from moshi.models import loaders, LMGen d = snapshot_download("BNarayanaReddy/siba", allow_patterns=["stage2b/checkpoint_001500/*", "stage2b/tokenizer.model"]) info = loaders.CheckpointInfo.from_hf_repo( "kyutai/moshiko-pytorch-bf16", # Mimi codec moshi_weights=f"{d}/stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/consolidated.safetensors", tokenizer=f"{d}/stage2b/tokenizer.model", config_path=f"{d}/stage2b/checkpoint_001500/consolidated/config.json", ) model = info.get_moshi(device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) mimi = info.get_mimi(device="cuda"); mimi.set_num_codebooks(8) lm_gen = LMGen(model, temp=0.8, temp_text=0.7, top_k=250, top_k_text=25) # Streaming as in Moshi: Mimi-encode the user's audio one 80 ms frame (1920 samples, 24 kHz) at a time; # lm_gen.step(codes) returns the model's text token + audio codes for that frame; mimi.decode() gives its speech. ``` ## Model details
Training data — 45,204 synthetic two-channel dialogues, 517 h | Language | Train hours | Script sources | Agent voice | User voices (vary per dialogue) | |---|:---:|---|---|---| | Hindi | 211 | samvaad-hi-v1, indic-align (Wiki_Conv, OpenAssistant_T), snorbyte | Ritvik | 120 IndicVoices speakers (60 male / 60 female) | | Telugu | 178 | indic-align (Wiki_Conv, OpenAssistant_T), Updesh, snorbyte | m3_te_s38 | 120 IndicVoices speakers (60 / 60) | | English | 128 | SODA, OpenAssistant | m3_en_s0 | 100 Svarah Indian-English speakers (50 / 50) | Scripts were cleaned (prompts and reasoning stripped, replies capped at ~50 words), voiced with the Maya 3 TTS, force-aligned (MMS) and assembled into two-channel conversations: median turn gap ~0.3 s, ~25% overlapping turn changes, barge-ins where the agent yields within ~0.27 s, and backchannels from a per-voice bank. Audio is Mimi-encoded at 8 codebooks per channel; 473 dialogues (5.6 h) are held out.
Training setup — 1,500 steps on 7 × H100, 31 min | Setting | Value | |---|---| | Init | Stage 1, step 15k (`stage1/checkpoint_015000`) | | Fine-tuning | full, Mimi frozen | | Batch | 49 × 60 s (0.82 h of audio per step), ~2.4 passes over the data | | Optimizer | AdamW, LR 2e-5, one-cycle with 5% warm-up, weight decay 0.1 | | Loss | agent text + agent audio (first codebook ×100, text padding ×0.5); the user channel is input only | | Language weights | Hindi 0.35 · Telugu 0.35 · English 0.30 | Exact config: [`stage2b/args.yaml`](stage2b/args.yaml) · eval log: [`stage2b/stage_eval.jsonl`](stage2b/stage_eval.jsonl) · benchmark reports: [`stage2b/bench/`](stage2b/bench)
Stage 1 (the base) Monologue speech from YouTube — Hindi 12.8k h, Telugu 12.1k h, English 8.4k h — with the user channel silent, so it is not conversational on its own. Checkpoints are in [`stage1/`](stage1) (5k, 10k, 15k; a continuation to 30k is in progress). Stage 2b starts from step 15k.
## Limitations - **Relevance.** Replies are often fluent but not about what the user asked, most of all in Hindi and Telugu. Understanding the user's speech is weak: Stage 1 never had a user channel and Stage 2b adds only ~500 h of listening. Hindi/Telugu knowledge answers can invent facts. - **Latency.** It responds 1.4–2 s after the user finishes, against ~0.3 s gaps in its training data. - **Synthetic data only.** All voices are TTS and the timing is rule-based; no real Hindi/Telugu conversations. Long-answer sources (OpenAssistant, Updesh) give few exchanges per minute. - **Evaluation.** Benchmark numbers are English only and from a 25% subset (components can move by ±0.1). - **Audio.** Moshi's 8-codebook Mimi on top of TTS audio limits clarity. ## Repository contents
All folders | Folder | What it is | |---|---| | `stage2b/` | this model: weights, config, tokenizer, training config, eval log, benchmark reports, card images | | `stage1/` | Stage 1 checkpoints with eval logs | | `moshiko_ext16k/` | the untrained starting point: Moshiko with the text vocabulary extended 32k → 48k | | `tokenizers/` | tokenizer candidates (table below) | | `configs/`, `scripts/`, `results/` | training configs, data and training scripts, evaluation reports | **moshiko_ext16k.** Ids 0–31999 are Moshi's original pieces (weights unchanged; English tokenises to identical ids); ids 32000–47999 are Telugu/Hindi pieces whose embedding and output rows start as the mean of the byte tokens they replace. The start-of-text row moved to 48000. On original-vocab input, audio logits and the first 32,000 text logits are bit-identical to Moshiko. Apply Unicode NFC to text before tokenising. | Tokenizer | Vocab | en tokens/word | hi tokens/word | te tokens/word | |---|---|---|---|---| | original Moshi | 32,000 | 1.28 | 10.70 | 19.66 | | **extend_16k (used)** | 48,000 | 1.278 | 1.23 | 1.53 | | extend_24k | 56,000 | 1.278 | 1.19 | 1.43 | | replace_32k | 32,000 | 1.34 | 1.20 | 1.46 |
## License and attribution Weights derive from Kyutai's Moshiko (CC-BY 4.0; copyright Kyutai, modified as described above). Training scripts come from SODA (CC-BY 4.0), sarvamai/samvaad-hi-v1 (Apache-2.0), ai4bharat indic-align, microsoft/Updesh and snorbyte samples (CC-BY 4.0); user voices were cloned from AI4Bharat's IndicVoices and Svarah. Check each source's terms before uses beyond research.
